extracted.intended_audience: poets, playwrights, and students of poetics/literary criticism
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for composing and evaluating tragic drama and epic poetry, covering plot construction, discovery/peripety, diction, metre, use of episodes, and the marvellous. Intended to shape how a poet/Playwright constructs action, language, and unity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Kinds of Discovery
rubrics_metrics.description: Discoveries may arise from signs and necklaces, from reasoning, or from the incidents themselves; the best Discoveries arise from the incidents themselves (a great surprise coming about through a probable incident).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: Oedipus and Iphigenia are best instances of discovery from incidents; composite discoveries from bad reasoning (e.g. Ulysses the False Messenger) are weaker. Discoveries independent of artifices (signs/necklaces) are superior; next best are those through reasoning.

rubrics_metrics.name: Visualize and stage the scenes (actor's-eye view)
rubrics_metrics.description: When constructing Plots and Diction, the poet should put the actual scenes as far as possible before his eyes and ‘act’ them with gestures.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Seeing events vividly like an eyewitness helps spot incongruities (e.g. failure in Carcinus where an on-stage incongruity offended spectators). As far as possible the poet should act his story with the very gestures of his personages so that emotions felt by the poet are convincingly portrayed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Simplify to a universal form before inserting episodes
rubrics_metrics.description: A story, whether already made or original, should first be simplified and reduced to a universal form, then lengthened by inserting episodes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: Iphigenia reduced to the universal element (maiden offered in sacrifice spirited away, later recognized by brother) before adding proper names and episodes. This ensures the core action is coherent before accessory incidents are added.

rubrics_metrics.name: Episodes must be appropriate and proportionate
rubrics_metrics.description: Inserted episodes or accessory incidents must be appropriate to the main action; in plays they should be short, in epic they may be used to lengthen the poem.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Appropriate episode example: fit of madness in Orestes which leads to arrest; inappropriate episodes (unmotivated or improbable intrusions) harm unity. In epic, episodes relieve uniformity (e.g. Odyssey’s Catalogue of Ships).

rubrics_metrics.name: Unity of action: single action with beginning, middle, and end
rubrics_metrics.description: The construction of a poem (including narrative verse) should be based on a single action that is a complete whole in itself, with a beginning, middle, and end, producing organic unity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Distinguish from history, which deals with a period of disconnected events. Homer exemplifies selection of a section rather than trying to cover an entire great event (e.g. not dramatizing the whole Trojan War).

rubrics_metrics.name: Complication and Denouement mastery
rubrics_metrics.description: Every tragedy is in part Complication (from start until the point just before the change in the hero's fortunes) and in part Denouement (from beginning of the change to the end); both must be properly constructed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Plots are compared chiefly by their Complication and Denouement. Many dramatists have good Complication but fail in Denouement; both aspects are necessary for a successful tragedy (example: Lynceus of Theodectes).

rubrics_metrics.name: Species of Tragedy and combining elements
rubrics_metrics.description: There are four species of Tragedy: (1) complex (Peripety and Discovery), (2) suffering, (3) character, and (4) spectacle; the poet should aim to combine every element of interest, or at least the more important ones.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: Ajaxes and Ixions (suffering); The Phthiotides and Peleus (character); The Phorcides and Prometheus (spectacle). Critics may expect a poet to surpass predecessors in multiple species, but the aim should be an integrated mix where feasible.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid dramatizing an epic body of incident
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not attempt to write a tragedy on an epic body of incident (a plurality of stories); dramatizing an entire epic-scale story typically ruins a play.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples of failure: dramatizing the whole Iliad or the whole Niobe story. Instead, select a portion suitable for dramatic treatment (Euripides and Aeschylus succeed by focusing on parts).

rubrics_metrics.name: Chorus as integral actor
rubrics_metrics.description: The Chorus should be regarded as one of the actors and take a share in the action—integral to the whole.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Sophocles’ Chorus is praised as appropriately integrated; later poets often make songs that have little to do with the Plot (intercalary pieces), which is a defect. Avoid treating choral songs as unrelated interludes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Thought expressed through language and action
rubrics_metrics.description: Thought (including attempts to prove/disprove, to arouse emotion, or to emphasize) is shown by characters' language and must align with their actions; actions make impressions without explanation whereas speech must produce the impression.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The mental procedure of characters should be consistent across their speech and actions. The spoken word must produce the impression deliberately; otherwise the speaker is useless if things appear in the required light without his words.

rubrics_metrics.name: Diction as composed of basic linguistic elements
rubrics_metrics.description: Diction comprises the Letter, the Syllable, the Conjunction, the Article, the Noun, the Verb, the Case, and the Speech—each with technical properties that affect poetic language.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ars/metre specialists handle technicalities like letter accent and syllable length. Understanding these components is part of mastering poetic diction (e.g., role of syllable in metre, noun/verb structures, and cases as modes of utterance).

rubrics_metrics.name: Perfection of Diction: clear and not mean
rubrics_metrics.description: The perfection of Diction is for it to be at once clear and not mean—balancing ordinary words (which give clearness) and unfamiliar terms (which give distinction).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Purely ordinary diction is clear but mean (prosaic); wholly unfamiliar diction becomes riddle or barbarism. A proper admixture (strange words, metaphors, ornamental forms, lengthened/curtailed words) prevents prosaic tone while maintaining clarity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Moderate use of metaphors, strange words, and word-forms
rubrics_metrics.description: Metaphors, strange words, lengthened/curtailed/altered forms should be used in moderation; excessive or improper use provokes laughter or produces barbarism or riddles.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Test substitutions by replacing poetic forms with ordinary words to see effects. Examples: Euripides’ small vocabulary change can improve a line. Too apparent use of licences (lengthening words excessively) has ludicrous effect, so the rule of moderation applies.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mastery of metaphor as sign of genius
rubrics_metrics.description: Being a master of metaphor is the greatest poetic achievement; a good metaphor implies intuitive perception of similarity in dissimilars and cannot be learned from others.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Metaphor elevates diction; it cannot be reduced to formulaic technique. Cultivate intuitive comparison and apt transference (genus↔species, species↔species, analogy).

rubrics_metrics.name: Word-choice by genre and metre
rubrics_metrics.description: Different kinds of words suit different poetic kinds: compounds fit the dithyramb, strange words heroic poetry, metaphors iambic; heroic poetry can use all of them.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Heroic metre tolerates strange words and metaphors best because of its gravity; iambic verse models speech and should limit itself to words allowable in oration (ordinary word, metaphor, ornamental equivalent).

rubrics_metrics.name: Epic: single action, similar parts to tragedy, and metre/length constraints
rubrics_metrics.description: Epic poetry should be based on a single action (with episodes as relief), include the same kinds of parts as tragedy (peripeties, discoveries, suffering), and obey length and metre constraints—be short enough to be grasped at once and use heroic metre.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Length: the poem should be shorter than the old epics, about as long as a series of tragedies for one hearing. Meter: heroic metre is appropriate; other metres create incongruity. Epic can describe simultaneous incidents not possible on stage, granting grandeur and variety.

rubrics_metrics.name: Poet's intradiegetic presence: minimize authorial intrusion
rubrics_metrics.description: The poet should say very little in propria persona; instead the poem should promptly introduce characters, each with distinctive characteristics.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Homer praised for brief preface then immediately introducing character-figures rather than frequent authorial interjections. The poet is an imitator; over-authorial presence diminishes imitation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of the marvellous and the improbable
rubrics_metrics.description: The marvellous is required in Tragedy; Epic affords more opening for the improbable. In all cases a likely impossibility is preferable to an unconvincing possibility.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If improbable incidents must occur, place them outside the piece (presupposed) rather than within it where they break credibility. Examples of misuse: report of Pythian games in Electra; man's silent journey in The Mysians. The Odyssey conceals improbabilities with other excellences.

rubrics_metrics.name: Elaborate diction only where no action or character
rubrics_metrics.description: Elaborate (ornate) diction is required only in places with no action and where no character or Thought is being revealed; otherwise it obscures them.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Where Character or Thought is present, over-ornate diction tends to obscure their effect. Use elevated diction sparingly and where it adds rather than hides meaning.

rubrics_metrics.name: Justify impossibilities by poetic ends or opinion; technical errors judged by relevance to art
rubrics_metrics.description: Impossibilities in description are faults unless they serve the poetic end (making some portion more astounding) or correspond to opinion or 'as ought to be'; technical errors in matters closely connected to the art are more serious than those only accidentally connected.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If poetic end could be achieved without sacrificing technical correctness, the impossibility is unjustified (lesser excuse if error is merely accidental to poetic art). Example: Pursuit of Hector could be defended for poetic effect, but avoid inaccuracies when they can be avoided without loss.

rubrics_metrics.name: Defences for poetical untruths: as they were/are/ought to be or opinion/custom
rubrics_metrics.description: When criticized for not being true to fact, a poet may argue he depicts things 'as they ought to be' (Sophocles) or 'as they were/are' or in accordance with prevailing opinion or custom.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Tales about gods may be defended as accordance with opinion; other statements may be defended by appeal to historical custom (e.g. arms stuck butt-end on ground) or by asserting the poet's moral/ideal representation of humans.

rubrics_metrics.name: Resolve linguistic/textual difficulties by multiple interpretive moves
rubrics_metrics.description: Apparent textual or linguistic faults can be addressed by assuming a strange word, treating an expression as metaphorical, changing reading mode, adjusting punctuation, assuming equivocal terms, or appealing to custom of language.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: interpreting Homeric terms metaphorically or by dialectal usage; re-punctuating Empedocles; recognizing equivocal meanings of words like pleo; appealing to custom (e.g. calling wine-and-water 'wine'). Critics' alleged errors sometimes stem from their own mistaken assumptions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of paralogism and rhetorical framing
rubrics_metrics.description: Framing of improbable antecedents by adducing believable consequents (paralogism) can be used to make a lie or marvellous event acceptable—adding B (a true/known consequent) to lead audience to infer A.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Homer’s craft includes such paralogism (Bath-story); use with care to make the improbable seem plausible. But prefer likely impossibility to unconvincing possibility and avoid internal contradictions that break audience belief.
